title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: The whole of that day Anna spent at home — that is, at the Oblonskys' — and received no one, though some of her acquaintances had already heard of her arrival and came to call that same day. Anna spent the whole morning with Dolly and the children. She sent only a brief note to her brother to tell him that he must not fail to come home for dinner. "Come, God is merciful," she wrote.

Oblonsky did dine at home; the conversation was general, and his wife, in speaking to him, addressed him as "Stiva," as she had not done before. The same estrangement still remained in the relations of husband and wife, but there was no talk now of separation, and Stepan Arkadyevitch saw the possibility of explanation and reconciliation.

Right after dinner Kitty came in. She knew Anna Arkadyevna, but only very slightly, and she came to her sister's now with some trepidation at the prospect of meeting this fashionable Petersburg lady whom everyone spoke so highly of. But she made a favorable impression on Anna Arkadyevna — she saw that at once. Anna was unmistakably admiring her loveliness and her youth; before Kitty knew where she was she found herself not only under Anna's sway but in love with her, the way young girls do fall in love with older married women. Anna was not like a fashionable lady, nor like the mother of an eight-year-old boy. In the elasticity of her movements, the freshness and unflagging eagerness that lingered in her face and broke out in her smile and her glance, she would rather have passed for a girl of twenty, were it not for a serious and at times sorrowful look in her eyes that struck Kitty and drew her in. Kitty felt that Anna was perfectly simple and was concealing nothing, but that she had another, higher world of interests, inaccessible to her, complex and poetic.
After dinner, when Dolly went off to her own room, Anna got up quickly and went over to her brother, who was just lighting a cigar.
"Stiva," she said to him, winking gaily, crossing him and glancing toward the door, "go on, and God help you."
He put down the cigar, understanding her, and walked off through the doorway.

When Stepan Arkadyevitch had disappeared, she went back to the sofa where she had been sitting, surrounded by the children. Either because the children saw that their mother was fond of this aunt, or because they felt some special charm in her themselves, the two elder ones, and the younger ones following their lead, as children so often do, had been clinging to their new aunt since before dinner and would not leave her side. And it had become a sort of game among them to sit as close to her as they could, to touch her, hold her little hand, kiss it, play with her ring, or even touch the flounce of her skirt.
"Come, come — as we were sitting before," said Anna Arkadyevna, taking her place again.
And again Grisha poked his little face under her arm and nestled his head against her gown, beaming with pride and happiness.
"And when is your next ball?" she asked Kitty.
"Next week, and a splendid ball. One of those balls where you always enjoy yourself."
"Are there really balls where you always enjoy yourself?" Anna said with tender irony.
"It's strange, but there are. At the Bobrishtchevs' you always enjoy yourself, and at the Nikitins' too, while at the Mezhkovs' it's always dull. Haven't you noticed?"

"No, my dear, for me there are no balls now where one enjoys oneself," said Anna, and Kitty caught in her eyes that mysterious world that was not open to her. "For me there are some less dull and tiresome than others."
"How can _you_ be dull at a ball?"
"Why shouldn't _I_ be dull at a ball?" Anna asked.
Kitty realized that Anna knew what answer was coming.
"Because you always look nicer than anyone."
Anna had the faculty of blushing. She blushed a little and said:
"In the first place, that's never the case; and secondly, if it were, what difference would it make to me?"
"Are you going to this ball?" asked Kitty.
"I imagine there'll be no avoiding it. Here, take it," she said to Tanya, who was pulling the loose ring off her white, slender-tipped finger.
"I should be so glad if you go. I'd so love to see you at a ball."

"At any rate, if I do go, I'll comfort myself with the thought that it gives you pleasure... Grisha, don't pull my hair. It's untidy enough as it is," she said, putting up a straying lock that Grisha had been playing with.
"I picture you at the ball in lilac."

"And why in lilac, particularly?" asked Anna, smiling. "Now, children, run along, run along. Do you hear? Miss Hoole is calling you to tea," she said, peeling the children off her and sending them off to the dining-room.
"I know why you're pressing me to come to the ball. You're expecting a great deal from this ball, and you want everyone to be there to share in it."
"How did you know? Yes."

"Oh, what a happy time you're at," Anna went on. "I remember it, and I know that blue haze, like the mist on the mountains in Switzerland. That mist that covers everything in that blissful time when childhood is just ending, and out of that vast circle, happy and gay, there is a path growing narrower and narrower, and it is both delightful and frightening to step into the ballroom, bright and splendid though it is... Who hasn't been through it?"
Kitty smiled without speaking. "But how did she get through it? How I'd love to know her whole love story," she thought, remembering Alexey Alexandrovitch's unromantic appearance — her husband.
"I know a little. Stiva told me, and I congratulate you. I liked him so much," Anna went on. "I met Vronsky at the railway station."
"Oh, was he there?" Kitty asked, blushing. "What did Stiva tell you?"

"Stiva gossiped about it all. And I'd be so glad... I traveled yesterday with Vronsky's mother," she went on; "and his mother talked without a stop about him, he's her favorite. I know mothers are partial, but..."
"What did his mother tell you?"

"Oh, a great deal! And I know he's her favorite; still, you can see how chivalrous he is... Well, for instance, she told me that he had wanted to give up all his property to his brother, that he had done something extraordinary when he was quite a child, saved a woman out of the water. He's a hero, in fact," said Anna, smiling and remembering the two hundred roubles he had given at the station.

But she didn't tell Kitty about the two hundred roubles. For some reason it was unpleasant to her to think about it. She felt that there was something in it that had to do with her, something that ought not to have been.

"She pressed me very much to come and see her," Anna went on; "and I'll be glad to go to her tomorrow. Stiva is staying a long time in Dolly's room, thank God," Anna added, changing the subject, and getting up, Kitty thought, displeased about something.
"No, I'm first! No, me!" the children screamed, having finished their tea, as they came running back to their Aunt Anna.
"All together," said Anna, and ran laughing to meet them, and embraced and swung around the whole crowd of swarming children, who shrieked with delight.
